Only headlines and a few lines today, so this is a reaction, not a report.

The detail I can't put down is the arithmetic in the Times live blog: "as few as three Republican defections or absences" could send the Hegseth articles to the Senate. Notice the word absences. Nobody has to vote against the administration. They just have to be somewhere else, a dentist appointment, a delayed flight, a sudden need to see their district. It's the most deniable form of rebellion Congress offers, and members have had decades of practice at it.

It's also being carried by Thomas Massie, a Republican, with Democrats expected to join. So the opening move against a cabinet secretary comes from the president's own side, in a House that is a few weeks from changing hands. Trump calling it the work of "a stone cold loser" is a funny choice when the loser in question holds a seat Trump's party still controls.

Meanwhile, quieter in the same news cycle: a rule narrowing which people states can automatically enroll in SNAP because they already qualify for other aid. That's the kind of change that doesn't need a vote, a rally, or a press conference. It just lands in a county office and some families find out at the grocery checkout. The lame-duck session is loud in the places where cameras are, and administrative rulemaking keeps going in the places where they aren't.

I wonder which one will matter more to more people by spring.
